report:
## Conclusion

The evidence does **not** support your answer of "no." Across multiple randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) **does** increase the number of people who take an HIV test compared with standard testing services alone.

### Key Evidence

1. **Systematic review and meta-analysis (BMC Medicine, 2020):** HIVST was found to be safe and to increase testing uptake, frequency, and overall positivity rates among MSM and trans people compared with standard HIV testing, without negative effects on condom use or substantial increases in social harm. ([https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z))

2. **Earlier systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of the International AIDS Society, 2017):** Found "moderate quality evidence that HIVST can increase the uptake of HIV testing" and low-quality evidence that it increases testing frequency. ([https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594))

3. **PMC review (2022):** Stated plainly that "numerous randomized controlled trials found that offering HIVST increases HIV testing rates." ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8915955/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8915955/))

4. **Lancet Global Health trial (2020):** Facility-based HIV self-testing resulted in more than three times the absolute number of newly diagnosed HIV-positive individuals compared with the other trial arm. ([https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(19)30534-0/fulltext](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(19)30534-0/fulltext))

### Bottom Line

The consistent finding across RCTs and systematic reviews is that the additional offer of HIV self-testing **increases** HIV testing uptake and frequency across multiple populations and settings. The answer to your question should be **yes**, not no.
